props.title: White Line Fever
props.initialSlug: Trucker fights corruption on deadly Arizona highways

sections.content: White Line Fever (1975) blazed a trail for the gritty trucking films of the 1970s, with Jan-Michael Vincent delivering a raw performance as Carrol Jo Hummer, a Vietnam vet fighting corruption in the trucking industry. The film taps into the decade's anti-establishment fury, much like Walking Tall (1973) and Billy Jack (1971), but shifts the action to America's highways. Director Jonathan Kaplan captures the dusty Arizona landscapes with a documentary-like realism that influenced later working-class revenge films like Fighting Mad (1976) and Rolling Thunder (1977).

sections.content: The film emerged during the CB radio craze of the mid-1970s, when trucking culture captured America's imagination. This zeitgeist produced hits like Smokey and the Bandit (1977) and Every Which Way But Loose (1978), though White Line Fever stands apart with its darker tone and social commentary. The film's exploration of corporate corruption and the independent trucker's struggle for survival resonated deeply during the 1973 oil crisis and subsequent economic instability.

Kay Lenz's performance as Carrol Jo's wife Jerri adds crucial emotional depth, elevating the film above typical revenge narratives. The relationship drama echoes similar working-class stories like Hard Times (1975) and Blue Collar (1978), where personal relationships strain under economic pressure. The film's stunning practical stunts, particularly the climactic truck battle, influenced later highway action sequences in films like The Road Warrior (1981). sections.content: White Line Fever helped establish a distinctly American strain of proletarian cinema that continued through films like F.I.S.T. (1978) and Norma Rae (1979). Its influence can be seen in later trucking films like Black Dog (1998) and Joy Ride (2001), though few matched its authentic portrayal of the trucking industry's challenges. The film's legacy lives on in modern working-class dramas like Nomadland (2020) and American Woman (2018).
